introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0550), Paper 2, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: Two and a Half Hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions choosing ONE from each section.

Question ONE carries 30 marks. All the other Questions carry 20 marks each.

Each question that is sub-divided has the sub marks in brackets.

In questions involving calculations, all steps of the working MUST be shown.

If an outline MAP and/or GRAPH are used, they must be tied inside your answer booklet, opposite the written part of the answer.

NB - ONLY THE FIRST FOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

(a) On the outline map of Cameroon provided, locate and name

- The central Industrial region

questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the outline map printed with the paper (shown above, with the north arrow at the top). Mark each feature at the right place and **write its name** beside it; add a key if you use different symbols (a dot for a point, a shaded area for a region). The positions are described in words relative to the outline (a small error is accepted).

| Item | What to name | Where on the outline map |
|---|---|---|
| **A rubber plantation** | **HEVECAM rubber estate (near Niete, south of Kribi)** | in the **South region**, in the south-west, not far from the Atlantic coast |
| | *or* a **CDC rubber estate** (for example near Tiko) | in the **South-West region**, at the foot of Mount Cameroon, on the coast |
| **The central industrial region** | **The Douala-Edea industrial region** (Littoral) | on the **Atlantic coast** at the head of the Wouri estuary (Douala) and the lower Sanaga valley (Edea, with its aluminium smelter), the main concentration of industries (the paper does not say which region is meant) |
| **One inland fishing ground** | **Lake Chad** (and the Logone floodplain) | in the **extreme north (Far North)**, at the top of the map |
| | *or* the **Lagdo reservoir** (River Benue) | in the **North region** |
| **Mount Cameroon** | **Mount Cameroon** (an active volcano, the highest mountain of Cameroon, about 4000 m high) | on the **south-west coast** (South-West region), north-west of Douala and close to the Gulf of Guinea; draw a small triangle and write its name |
| **Any one dam** | **Lagdo dam** (River Benue, hydroelectricity and irrigation) | in the **North region** |
| | *or* the **Edea and Song Loulou dams** (River Sanaga) | in the **Littoral**, inland from Douala |

**Marking guide (6 marks).** For each feature: 1 mark for the correct position (the name is required to get the mark). Five features are listed, so a candidate who locates and names them all correctly may have one mark in reserve (the total is limited to 6).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Name THREE forest resources
(ii) Briefly describe FOUR ways by which forest resources can be conserved

(3 + 4 = 7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Three forest resources (3 marks, 1 mark each).**

1. **Timber** (hardwoods such as mahogany, iroko, ebony, sapele and obeche), used for building, furniture and export.
2. **Fuelwood** (firewood) and charcoal, the main source of energy for cooking in many homes.
3. **Non-timber forest products:** fruits and seeds (bush mango, njansang), leaves (eru, okok), honey, rattan and bamboo, **medicinal plants** and bush meat (the wildlife of the forest).

(Other correct resources: rubber latex, water and soil protection, tourism and the forest as a habitat for wildlife.)

**(ii) Four ways of conserving forest resources (4 marks, 1 mark each: the way and a short description).**

1. **Reforestation and afforestation:** planting trees to replace those that were cut and on bare land, so that the forest area is kept or restored.
2. **Selective and controlled logging (sustainable management):** felling only mature trees of a given size, within **quotas** and in rotation, and using forest management plans so that the forest can regenerate.
3. **Protected areas:** creating **national parks, forest reserves and wildlife sanctuaries**, and **community forests** managed by villages, where cutting and hunting are forbidden or controlled (for example Korup and Dja).
4. **Laws and their enforcement:** the **forestry law**, the control of logging companies, the fight against **illegal logging and poaching** with forest guards and penalties, and the control of bush fires.
5. **Education and alternatives:** educating villagers about the value of the forest, and offering alternatives such as **improved cooking stoves**, **agroforestry** and the use of other energy so that people cut less fuelwood.

(Any four are enough.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) List FOUR Touristic potentials in Cameroon.
(ii) Briefly describe THREE challenges facing the Tourism Industry

(2 + 5 = 7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Four tourist potentials of Cameroon (2 marks, half a mark each).**

1. **Mount Cameroon**, a volcano that attracts climbers and hikers (including the annual race on the mountain).
2. **Beaches** on the Atlantic coast (Limbe, Kribi) and the **Lobe waterfalls** at Kribi, which fall into the sea.
3. **National parks and wildlife reserves**, such as Waza (Far North), Benoue (North), Korup (South-West) and Dja (South), with their elephants, antelopes, lions and primates.
4. **Culture and traditional chiefdoms:** the palaces and museums of Foumban and Bafut, traditional festivals and handicrafts.
5. Other potentials: the **crater lakes** (Barombi Mbo, Oku), the Limbe Botanic Garden and Wildlife Centre, the Mandara Mountains and waterfalls such as Ekom-Nkam.

(Any four are enough.)

**(ii) Three challenges facing the tourism industry (5 marks: 1 mark for each challenge and a description, with 2 marks for the best developed; any three).**

1. **Poor infrastructure.** Many tourist sites are reached by bad roads, there are not enough good hotels, and electricity, water supply and communications are unreliable, so many tourists are discouraged.
2. **Insecurity.** Armed conflicts and attacks in some regions (the North-West and South-West regions and the Far North) make visitors afraid and cause a fall in the number of tourists.
3. **Insufficient publicity and poor management.** The tourist sites are not well known abroad and are badly advertised; the management of the sites is often weak and corruption and harassment at the borders and on the roads discourage visitors.
4. **High cost and entry formalities.** Air tickets and hotels are expensive and the visa procedures are slow and complicated.
5. **Shortage of trained staff and degradation of the environment.** Few guides and hotel workers are well trained, and poaching, deforestation and rubbish spoil the attractions.
